questiontext.text:
There are three lotteries in town:

BIG WIN: costs £{@dispdp(float(bigWinCost),2)@} per ticket and the chance of winning £{@bigWinPrize@} is {@float(bigWinRate*100)@}%.

LITTLE LUCKY: costs {@littleLuckyCostFrac@} of the price of BIG WIN per ticket, and the chance of winning £{@littleLuckyPrize@} is {@float(littleLuckyRate)@}.

ALL IN ONE: costs £{@allInOneTicketNo*allInOneCost@} for {@allInOneTicketNo@} tickets, and the chance of winning £{@allInOnePrize@} on a single ticket is {@allInOneRate@}.

(4)

Which lottery gives you the most profit-per-prize on average?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

How much profit is it?

£ [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

[[feedback:prt1]]

truefeedback.text:
Here is a worked solution:

BIG WIN:

The chance of winning in this lottery is \({@float(bigWinRate*100)@}\% = {@bigWinRate@}\) so we should expect to win, on average, once in every \(\frac{{@1@}}{({@bigWinRate@})} = {@1/bigWinRate@}\) tickets.

This means that for every \(£{@bigWinPrize@}\) that you win, on average you will have spent \({@1/bigWinRate@} \times £{@dispdp(bigWinCost,2)@} = £{@dispdp(bigWinCost/bigWinRate,2)@}\).

This gives an average win-per-prize of \(£{@bigWinPrize@} - £{@dispdp(bigWinCost/bigWinRate,2)@} = {@if bigWinProfit<0 then "-" else ""@}£{@dispdp(abs(bigWinProfit),2)@}\).


LITTLE LUCKY:

The chance of winning in this lottery is \({@float(littleLuckyRate)@} = {@littleLuckyRate@}\) so we should expect to win, on average, once in every \(\frac{{@1@}}{({@littleLuckyRate@})} = {@1/littleLuckyRate@}\) tickets.

Each ticket costs \({@dispdp(bigWinCost,2)@} \times {@littleLuckyCostFrac@} = {@dispdp(littleLuckyCost,2)@}\). This means that for every \(£{@littleLuckyPrize@}\) that you win, on average you will have spent \({@1/littleLuckyRate@} \times £{@dispdp(littleLuckyCost,2)@} = £{@dispdp(littleLuckyCost/littleLuckyRate,2)@}\).

This gives an average win-per-prize of \(£{@littleLuckyPrize@} - £{@dispdp(littleLuckyCost/littleLuckyRate,2)@} = {@if littleLuckyProfit<0 then "-" else ""@}£{@dispdp(abs(littleLuckyProfit),2)@}\).


ALL IN ONE:

The chance of winning in this lottery is {@allInOneRate@} so we should expect to win, on average, once in every \(\frac{{@1@}}{({@allInOneRate@})} = {@1/allInOneRate@}\) tickets.

The the cost of each ticket is \(\frac{£{@allInOneCost*allInOneTicketNo@}}{{@allInOneTicketNo@}} = £{@dispdp(allInOneCost,2)@}\). This means that for every \(£{@allInOnePrize@}\) that you win, on average you will have spent \({@1/allInOneRate@} \times £{@dispdp(allInOneCost,2)@} = £{@dispdp(allInOneCost/allInOneRate,2)@}\).

This gives an average win-per-prize of \(£{@allInOnePrize@} - £{@dispdp(allInOneCost/allInOneRate,2)@} = {@if allInOneProfit<0 then "-" else ""@}£{@dispdp(abs(allInOneProfit),2)@}\).


This means that {@bestLottery@} has the highest profit-per-prize at \({@if bestProfit<0 then "-" else ""@}£{@dispdp(abs(bestProfit),2)@}\).

falsefeedback.text:
You are correct that {@ans1@} is lottery with the largest profit-per-prize.
However, the profit-per-prize is not \({@if ans2<0 then "-" else ""@}£{@dispdp(abs(ans2),2)@}\).

truefeedback.text:
You have correctly calculated the best profit-per-prize of the three lotteries.
However, the lottery which gives this profit-per-prize is {@bestLottery@}.

You have correctly calculated the profit-per-prize of {@ans1@}.
However, this is not the largest profit-per-prize of the three lotteries.
You may have calculated the expected profit-per-ticket of {@ans1@} instead of the profit-per-prize.

You may have treated the percentage \({@float(100*bigWinRate)@}\%\) as the fraction \(\frac{1}{{@float(100*bigWinRate)@}}\) when it is actually \(\frac{{@float(100*bigWinRate)@}}{100} = {@bigWinRate@}\) or \({@float(bigWinRate)@}\).
Remember that you can read a \(\%\) sign as "over 100".

You may have treated the decimal \({@float(littleLuckyRate)@}\) as the fraction \(\frac{1}{{@100*littleLuckyRate@}}\) when it is actually \(\frac{{@100*littleLuckyRate@}}{100} = {@littleLuckyRate@}\).
You may have treated the fraction \({@allInOneRate@}\) as the decimal \({@float(1/(100*allInOneRate))@}\) when it is actually \({@float(allInOneRate)@}\).
